articles.title: Do families in Oslo avoid neighbourhoods with non-Western immigrants?
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Those living in Oslo have long perceived the city's distinct residential divisions, and new academic research now provides data to back up those impressions.

A study by researchers at NOVA at Oslo Metropolitan University, published by forskning.no, investigated how families in the capital region choose where to live, revealing clear patterns.

Using data from over 20,000 family moves between 1993 and 2017, the study showed that despite city policies to encourage integration, families’ choices still lead to demographic divisions in Oslo.

​Specifically, Norwegian-born parents from all income and wealth levels avoid moving to neighbourhoods with high proportions of non-Western immigrants.

​Lead researcher Professor Lena Magnusson Turner said this trend is worrying. “Although policy facilitates people from different socio-economic classes living in the same neighbourhood, we see that the population chooses differently.”

​Turner explained that people also look for neighbours who are similar to themselves, while less affluent families actively avoid areas where they would feel financially inferior.

“When people move and have the opportunity to choose, they move to neighbourhoods where they find people who are like them. People don't seek out neighbourhoods where the inequalities are too great,” she said.

​The study also established that accumulated wealth influences neighbourhood selection far more than income, leading the most affluent households to cluster in specific areas.

​When looking at families with children, the study revealed that parents with daughters care more about the economic status of their neighbours than parents with sons. “We think it's about ideas parents have about protecting their girls to a greater extent, while assuming boys can handle themselves,” Turner added.

articles.title: Russlands ambassade nevner atomvåpen i uttalelse om Norge
articles.content:
Russlands ambassade i Oslo advarer om at norsk våpenproduksjon for Ukraina øker sikkerhetsrisikoen for Norge og viser til atomvåpen i sin uttalelse.

Bakgrunnen er en tilsvarende advarsel fra Russlands ambassadør i Danmark, som hevdet at dansk produksjon av militært materiell for Ukraina har økt sikkerhetsrisikoen for landet.

NRK har vært i kontakt med den russiske ambassaden som ikke ønsker å kommentere saken.

Norge inngikk tidligere i år en avtale med Ukraina om produksjon av ukrainske droner på norsk jord. Den russiske ambassaden i Oslo skriver til Nettavisen at slik produksjon tvinger Russland til mottiltak.

– Masseproduksjon, levering og bruk av slike våpen tvinger den russiske siden til å iverksette strenge og effektive mottiltak og fører til en eskalering av konflikten, noe som øker risikoen for at den utvides og til slutt kan føre til en direkte militær konflikt i Europa med katastrofale konsekvenser, skriver ambassaden.

De advarer videre om konsekvensene av en storskala konflikt mellom Russland og Nato.

– Trenger det å forklares at en eventuell storstilt konflikt mellom Russland og Nato, som begge besitter enorme kjernefysiske kapasiteter, og som utløses av fiendtlige handlinger fra en aggressiv blokk, bør betraktes som en betydelig sikkerhetsrisiko ikke bare for Norge og Europa, men for hele menneskeheten? skriver ambassaden.

Forholdet Norge – Russland

Forholdet mellom Norge og Russland er på et lavpunkt etter at Russland invaderte Ukraina i fjor. Norge deltar i sanksjonene mot Russland. I april 2023 erklærte Norge 15 ansatte ved den russiske ambassaden i Oslo som uønsket i Norge.

articles.title: Russia demands 'immediate release' of vessel seized by Norway
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Russia on Thursday demanded the "immediate release" of a Russian ship seized by Norway a day earlier in the Arctic at the demand of Ukrainian state energy group Naftogaz as compensation for asset seizures.

The governor of Svalbard, a Norwegian archipelago located 1,000 kilometres (621 miles) south of the North Pole, announced the seizure of the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, on Wednesday, September 2nd, citing an August 31st court order.

Naftogaz is seeking $4.2 billion from Russia as compensation for the seizure of its assets following Moscow's 2014 annexation of Crimea.

In 2023, a Hague-based arbitration tribunal ruled in favour of the Ukrainian company, a ruling Norway recognises.

The Professor Molchanov, a research vessel primarily used for expedition cruises, is currently stuck at the quay in Barentsburg, a mining settlement operated by Russia in Svalbard, pending a new decision by the governor or by the Norwegian courts, the governor's office said.

The Russian foreign ministry on Thursday said it had summoned the Norwegian ambassador to Russia, Heidi Olufsen, to lodge a "strong protest" over the seizure.

She was "informed that the Russian side categorically rejects not only the seizure of the Professor Molchanov but also the recent intensification of Norway's actions aimed at curtailing the legitimate Russian presence on the archipelago", the ministry said.

The Russian embassy in Norway condemned what it called "a politically motivated violation of international law" and announced it would lodge an appeal.

"We demand the immediate release of the vessel and that the safety of the passengers and crew be ensured," the embassy said in an email to AFP.

Norwegian authorities meanwhile said they are not "a party" in the case.

"As the authority responsible for enforcing court decisions, the governor of Svalbard is obliged to implement the court's ruling," Norwegian justice ministry spokesperson Frank Lynum told AFP.

"This applies to all cases of attachment and enforcement, regardless of the parties involved," he added, saying the issue was handled "in the ordinary way by the Norwegian courts".

Because of sanctions imposed by Norway after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, the seized vessel is, according to the Russian embassy, the only supply channel for Russian settlements in Svalbard.

The Arctic archipelago is governed by a 1920 treaty.

While it recognises Norwegian sovereignty, the treaty also grants nationals of all the contracting parties the right to exploit natural resources there "on a footing of absolute equality".

Russia operates a coal mine in the village of Barentsburg, where around 350 Russian and Russian-speaking Ukrainian residents live, as well as another smaller settlement called Pyramiden.

Oslo stresses that the rights guaranteed by the treaty do not exempt other nationals or companies from complying with Norwegian laws and regulations.

articles.title: Norway's UDI immigration authority website hit by cyberattack
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        The website of the Norwegian Directorate of Immigration (UDI) went offline on Friday, September 4th, after a cyberattack claimed by a pro-Russian hacker group.

The group, calling itself "Server Killers", claimed responsibility for the Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack, Norwegian media reported.

A DDoS attack occurs when multiple systems flood a target website with excessive traffic, causing the website to crash or become unavailable.

This incident comes at a time of growing concern about cybersecurity and threats aimed at public sector online services in recent weeks.

People attempting to access the official portal are met with error messages.

articles.title: Today in Norway: A roundup of the latest news on Friday
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        Støre maintains lead over Frp leader Sylvi Listhaug, families in Oslo avoid neighbourhoods with many non-Western immigrants, and more news from Norway on Friday.

Støre maintains lead in preferred prime minister poll

Although the Progress Party (Frp) has become the largest party in several recent polls, voters still favour current Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre from the Labour Party over opposition leader Sylvi Listhaug.

The latest InFact survey for Nettavisen shows Støre with 31.9 percent support, while Listhaug has 27.3 percent. Conservative Party candidate Ine Eriksen Søreide is in third place with 12.5 percent.

Although Støre is ahead, political analysts said that the 4.6 percentage point gap between him and Listhaug is too small to be statistically significant. This means the race is still very close, and the data does not show a clear lead for Støre.

This result is very different from recent party polls by Nettavisen, which show the right-wing Progress Party as the largest party with 31.4 percent, far ahead of Labour’s 22 percent.

Vegard Jarness, head of analysis at InFact, explained that Støre attracts support from a wider range of voters.

“The difference lies primarily in the candidates' ability to appeal outside their own party. Støre has far broader support across party lines,” Jarness said.

Norwegian vocabulary: målingen - the poll / Statsministermåling - prime minister poll

Norwegian economy remains resilient despite global trade tensions

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has concluded its annual assessment of Norway, reporting that the national economy remains resilient and well equipped to handle a demanding international situation despite ongoing geopolitical unrest and trade tensions.

The IMF expects Norway’s mainland economy to keep growing at a normal pace. Rising real wages and a strong labour market should continue to support private spending, as outlined in a press release from the Government.

However, inflation is expected to remain above target. The IMF stressed that economic policy must prioritise bringing inflation down without weakening economic activity more than necessary.

To keep the economy strong in the long run, the report suggests making changes to boost productivity and get more people into the workforce. The IMF especially urges the government to address the rising number of young workers joining long-term benefit schemes.

The report also recommends simplifying the tax system, and expanding the tax base, using the recent Tax Commission proposals as a good starting point for changes.

Norwegian vocabulary: motstandsdyktig - resilient / resistant

Russia demands 'immediate release' of vessel seized by Norway

Russia demanded the "immediate release" of a Russian ship seized by Norway on Wednesday, September 2nd, in the Arctic at the demand of Ukrainian state energy group Naftogaz as compensation for asset seizures.

The governor of Svalbard announced the seizure of the vessel, the Professor Molchanov, citing an August 31st court order.

The Russian foreign ministry on Thursday said it had summoned the Norwegian ambassador to Russia, Heidi Olufsen, to lodge a "strong protest" over the seizure.

She was "informed that the Russian side categorically rejects not only the seizure of the Professor Molchanov but also the recent intensification of Norway's actions aimed at curtailing the legitimate Russian presence on the archipelago", the ministry said.

The Russian embassy in Norway condemned what it called "a politically motivated violation of international law" and announced it would lodge an appeal.

"We demand the immediate release of the vessel and that the safety of the passengers and crew be ensured," the embassy said in an email to AFP.

Norwegian authorities meanwhile said they are not "a party" in the case.

"As the authority responsible for enforcing court decisions, the governor of Svalbard is obliged to implement the court's ruling," Norwegian justice ministry spokesperson Frank Lynum told AFP.

"This applies to all cases of attachment and enforcement, regardless of the parties involved," he added, saying the issue was handled "in the ordinary way by the Norwegian courts".

Norwegian vocabulary: kalle inn - to summon / to call in

Study finds Oslo families avoid neighbourhoods with many non-Western immigrants

A study by researchers at NOVA at Oslo Metropolitan University found that Norwegian-born parents from all income and wealth levels avoid moving to Oslo neighbourhoods with many non-Western immigrants.

Using data from over 20,000 family moves between 1993 and 2017, the study, published in the Journal of Urban Affairs, showed that despite city policies to encourage integration, families’ choices still lead to demographic divisions in Oslo.

"When people move and have the opportunity to choose, they move to neighbourhoods where they find people who are like them. People don't seek out neighbourhoods where the inequalities are too great," said lead researcher Professor Lena Magnusson Turner.

The study also established that accumulated wealth influences neighbourhood selection far more than income, leading the most affluent households to cluster in specific areas.

Researchers also found that families with daughters cared more about the economic status of their neighbours than families with sons.

Norwegian vocabulary: ikke-vestlige innvandrere - non-Western immigrants / å unngå -  to avoid

Deliveries to Rema 1000, one of Norway’s biggest supermarket chains, could stop on the morning of Saturday September 5th, as 700 warehouse and distribution workers prepare for a potential strike.

Trade unions Fellesforbundet and Yrkestrafikkforbundet have until midnight Friday to reach a deal with the Confederation of Norwegian Enterprise (NHO) on the national wholesale agreement.

If mediation fails, 411 Rema Distribusjon staff will walk out, affecting supermarket supplies across the country, as well as deliveries to Thon Hotels and Felleskjøpet.

"We have no intention of hitting third parties, but a strike will necessarily have consequences. For Rema 1000, a halt in the flow of goods will quickly be felt on store shelves", Fellesforbundet lead negotiator Mohammed Malik told news outlet E24.

The unions want higher purchasing power and for employers to pay sick, care, and parental benefits directly to staff, so workers do not have to wait for payments from the Norwegian Labour and Welfare Administration (NAV).

articles.title: Inside ModUlf: How Norway is rebuilding its immigration system
articles.content:
Add The Local as a preferred source
    
                        
                                        
                        If you are wondering whether Norwegian immigration authorities truly want to improve their processes, let us tell you about ModUlf, a six-year project that aims to change the harsh reality faced by people who endure long waits during their migration process in Norway. Will it succeed?

Anyone who has moved to Norway knows the process can be tough. There are strict rules, confusing steps, and long waits that feel like a struggle against old, slow systems.

In previous interviews, the Directorate of Immigration (UDI) has acknowledged these structural flaws. They have especially pointed out the outdated technology, which has forced them to rethink and redesign their infrastructure.

To combat the challenges, they are currently developing the project ModUlf (Modernisert utlendingsforvaltning – Modernised Immigration Administration), a six-year digitalisation programme that started in 2025.

To understand how Norway is quietly rebuilding its entire immigration system, The Local spoke with Henrik Hansen, the Product Lead (Produktleder) working in ModUlf within the "Staying in Norway and Becoming Norwegian" phase.

ModUlf, as the authorities present it on their website, is “our chance to shape the future of immigration administration.”

It is a joint, comprehensive digitalisation programme uniting the four main authorities responsible for foreign nationals in Norway: the Directorate of Immigration (UDI), the Immigration Appeals Board (UNE), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (UD), and the police.

Through this multi-agency collaboration, their goal is to “create user-friendly, efficient and secure services – for the benefit of applicants, employees and society,” as stated on their website.

Norway's current migration system is outdated and was built for a different time. Hansen told The Local that they are working with old platforms from the early 2000s, which is the main reason for starting ModUlf.

"The main goal of the project is, of course, to have safe and stable systems, because that's the core mission that we're supposed to deliver," he said.

"But we don't just want to make exactly the same as we have now; it needs to be more modern. We also want to make something that is future-proof, and of course, gives us more value. By 'value,' we refer to shorter waiting times, a quicker and easier job for our workers, and of course, for the applicants."

According to the official ModUlf framework, most of the current software was built when digital threats were less advanced, there were fewer cases, and agencies worked separately. Over time, these old systems have been patched and changed so much that they are now very complex and make daily work harder.

The old technical systems also create security risks in today's world, while making it increasingly difficult for applicants to get help, creating a poor experience for foreign residents.

Immigration authorities acknowledged that caseworkers do not have enough time for their core work because slow, confusing systems force them to perform many manual tasks (one of the primary reasons processing times are so notoriously long).

Data is also spread across different systems that do not connect, so officials lack the necessary insights to make efficient decisions.

Hansen emphasised that stabilising this fragile foundation was the absolute priority for the state.

"Our main task is to get us more stable, modern, and safe systems," Hansen said.

"We wanted to improve the systems, and it was required because they are quite old. We want to ensure we can make the improvements we want in the future... We need a very good foundation. The system is very old, so it really requires an upgrade to make sure that our platforms are safe and stable," he said.

READ MORE: Inside ModUlf: What's changing in Norway's immigration process?

Upgrading a system of this scale is a delicate operation that must be carried out over an extended period.

Since replacing everything at once is not possible, experts like Hansen are slowly and gradually building new digital components around the old software. They remove old features step by step, while everyday operations continue uninterrupted, as usual, in the background.

"This is a project that will go over several years. There are a lot of things going on, and we can't do everything at the same time," Hansen said.

For this reason, the ModUlf programme has been broken down into four distinct, overlapping development streams stretching until 2031.

Stream 1 - Staying in Norway and becoming Norwegian (2025 – 2029): The first phase focuses on residents already established in the country, covering citizenship (statsborgerskap), permanent residence (permanent opphold), and permit renewals (fornyelse).

Stream 2 - Coming to Norway (2026 – 2030): The second phase focuses on the entry and initial relocation, including visitor visas, family immigration (familieinnvandring), work permits, and study permits.

Stream 3 - Protection and asylum (2027 – 2030): The third phase upgrades the distinct casework pathways required for those seeking international protection.

Stream 4 - Sanctions and departures (2028 – 2031): The final stream focuses on enforcement systems, including the management of expulsions (utvisning), deportations (bortvisning), and the revocation of citizenship or legal status.

Hansen explained that while some features within the ModUlf project are tailored strictly to each specific phase, like citizenship, others are designed as shared infrastructure.

READ ALSO: 'We truly understand that anxiety': The human side of Norway’s immigration system upgrade

“This means, for example, that when we start with permanent residency, we will have some parts, like systems and features, already made from the previous advances in citizenship that can also be used for this, and we can focus on the more specific parts of permanent residency," he said.

"This helps with making systems that are interconnected and consistent."

At first, it may seem odd that the timeline goes in the opposite order of a typical immigrant's journey to Norway from arriving to becoming part of it. However, Hansen explained the clear reasoning behind this choice.

“We actually go backward. We have started with citizenship. It is the last part of the journey in becoming Norwegian and being in Norway, but because we already had a lot of information about people at this stage, we started with that," said Hansen.

Starting at the end of the process lets the team build a strong foundation using data the state already has and trust. "The 'Staying in Norway' phase is considered an easier area, not because it's simple, but because we have a lot of data from before, so we can use that information to make robust systems," Hansen said.

In contrast, opening up the initial application pipeline for newcomers presents far greater technical and analytical hurdles.

“The 'Coming to Norway' phase is a much bigger part, which we have broken up into multiple deliveries because it's very complicated. When you come to Norway, you're usually here for the first time. So, it requires quite different ways of working with those types of cases. We need much more information," explained Hansen.

As for the final enforcement stream, it might seem unique to mix it with general immigration services, but Hansen pointed out that it represents a vital part of managing the overall system.

However, it requires a completely distinct administrative approach: "It is different because that is something the authorities start on their own; it's not something an applicant applies for."

articles.title: Støre åpner Yara-anlegg i «sørgeperioden»
articles.content:
Statsminister Jonas Gahr Støres planlagte tur til Nederland gjennomføres mandag 7. september. Beslutningen tas midt i den nasjonale sørgeperioden etter kong Haralds død.

NRK stilte tre spørsmål til Statsministerens kontor vedrørende besøket, deriblant hvorfor reisen gjennomføres midt i en nasjonal sørgeperiode som regjeringen selv har tatt initiativ til.

Statssekretær Bhanuja Rasiah opplyser til NRK at reisen ble planlagt før kong Harald døde.

– Reisen til Nederland gjennomføres som planlagt, men programmet gjenspeiler at Norge er i en nasjonal sørgeperiode. Det blir blant annet ett minutts stillhet på Yaras anlegg i Sluiskil, og flagging på halv stang hos Yara og ved Middelburg kloster.

Drivstoffprisene skyter mot 30 kroner literen, uten at politikerne vil uttale seg om prissjokket. Senterpartiet forsøkte å samle de andre partiene for å lempe på den politiske sørgepausen, men møtte stengte dører.

Kongefamilien

Kong Harald er død. Han sovnet stille inn på Rikshospitalet klokken 06.35 fredag 28. august 2026. Kong Haakon VIII tar valgspråket «Alt for Norge».

articles.title: Justisdepartementet om russisk skip i arrest på Svalbard
articles.content:
– Dette er en sak mellom Naftogaz og Russland. Norge er ikke part i saken. Det sier seniorrådgiver Frank Lynum i Justisdepartementet om arresten av det russiske skipet på Svalbard.

Etter begjæring fra Naftogaz har tingretten besluttet at det skal tas arrest i skipet.

– Som namsfogd er Sysselmesteren forpliktet til å gjennomføre avgjørelsen fra Nord-Troms og Senja tingrett. Det gjelder alle saker om arrest og utlegg, uavhengig av hvem som er parter. Tingretten har tatt avgjørelsen uten først å orientere Russland, sier Lynum.

Som part i saken kan Russland kreve at tingretten vurderer saken på nytt.

– Det har Russland gjort i en tidligere sak om utlegg. I rollen som namsfogd har Sysselmesteren fulgt opp det Nord-Troms og Senja tingrett har bestemt, akkurat som namsfogden ville gjort dersom dette skjedde på fastlandet, sier Lynum.

Den russiske skyggeflåten

Skyggeflåten er et nettverk av oljetankere og lasteskip som Russland bruker for å forbigå vestlige sanksjoner. De er ofte privateide og seiler gjerne under ulike flagg. Det er ofte vanskelig å spore eierene.

articles.content:

Et betydelig antall politipatruljer er satt inn i området. Politiet samler inn opplysninger og gjennomfører tekniske undersøkelser.

Politiet ber personer som har hørt smell eller skudd i messeområdet eller Tønsberg sentrum mellom midnatt og 1.45, om å ta kontakt.

Ingen er så langt pågrepet etter at en mann ble skutt i Tønsberg i natt. Den skadde er fløyet til sykehus med alvorlige skader.

articles.content:

Ved utgangen av uke 35 var fyllingsgraden 45,9 prosent. Det er det laveste siden 1996 da fyllingsgraden var 46,1 prosent i samme uke.

Analytikere avisen har snakket med frykter høye strømpriser hvis det blir en tørr høst og kald vinter.

De siste to årene har strømprisen i store deler av landet vært uvanlig høy. Markedsprisen på strøm kan følges fra time til time på strømbørsen Nord Pool.
